title: Area V review: Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area V: steep turns, the steep spiral, chandelles, lazy eights and eights on pylons. Many compare two maneuvers you may fly on the same checkride flight, since the examiner picks one from each pair plus eights on pylons.

questions.q: Your examiner briefs Area V of your initial commercial ASEL checkride. Which set of maneuvers could the examiner pick?
options: Steep Turns, Chandelles and Lazy Eights
Steep Turns, Steep Spiral and Eights on Pylons
Steep Turns and Chandelles only
Steep Spiral, Lazy Eights and Eights on Pylons
questions.why: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant the evaluator must select Steep Turns or Steep Spiral, Chandelles or Lazy Eights, and Eights on Pylons (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). So every set needs one maneuver from each pair plus eights on pylons. A set without eights on pylons is wrong, and Steep Turns with Steep Spiral leaves out the chandelle or lazy eight. Eights on pylons is the most advanced of the ground reference maneuvers [[24:160|AFH 7-14]], so it is never skipped.

questions.q: Your airplane stalls at 52 knots at 1 G. On one flight you fly a 50° steep turn and a chandelle at 30° of bank, both coordinated. Using the level-turn rule, about how much higher is the stall speed in the steep turn than in the 30° bank?
options: About 13 knots
None, since stall speed depends only on weight
About 9 knots
About 4 knots
questions.why: In a level turn the load factor is the same for a given bank in any airplane, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. At 50°: 1 / cos 50° = 1.556, square root 1.247, 52 x 1.247 = 64.9 knots. At 30°: 1 / cos 30° = 1.155, square root 1.075, 52 x 1.075 = 55.9 knots. The difference is 64.9 - 55.9 = 9.0 knots. 13 knots is the rise from wings level to the 50° turn, not the gap to the 30° bank. 'None' is wrong because above 1 G the airplane stalls at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: The field below your practice area is at 1,200 feet MSL. You start a steep spiral at 4,800 feet MSL, and your first lap cost 650 feet. If each lap costs the same, how does your plan stand against the ACS?
options: Three turns fit, but you finish below 1,500 feet AGL
Only two full turns fit before 1,500 feet AGL
Three full turns fit, finishing about 1,650 feet AGL
Five full turns fit, since you start 3,600 feet above the field
questions.why: The ACS asks for at least three 360° turns, finishing no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S2, S6) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Room above the floor: 4,800 - 1,200 - 1,500 = 2,100 feet. 2,100 / 650 = 3.2, so three full turns fit. Three turns cost 3 x 650 = 1,950 feet, leaving 4,800 - 1,950 = 2,850 feet MSL, which is 2,850 - 1,200 = 1,650 feet AGL. 'Five turns' divides the whole 3,600 feet by 650 and ignores the 1,500-foot floor. Noting the altitude lost each lap is the AFH's planning tool [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: On a windy day you fly a steep spiral and later eights on pylons. In each one, what do you change as your heading swings toward downwind?
options: Spiral: steepen the bank. Eights: climb, because the pivotal altitude rises
Spiral: shallow the bank. Eights: descend
Both: steepen the bank to hold a constant radius
Spiral: hold the bank. Eights: steepen the bank
questions.why: The steep spiral is a constant radius turn, so you steepen the bank on downwind headings and shallow it on upwind headings [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Eights on pylons does not need a constant radius, so no drift correction is applied in the turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Its pivotal altitude is set by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]], and as groundspeed changes you climb or descend to hold the line on the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Downwind means more groundspeed, so climb. 'Both steepen the bank' treats the eight like a constant radius maneuver, which it is not.

questions.q: Where is the airspeed lowest in a chandelle, and where in a lazy eight?
options: Chandelle: at the 180° point, wings level. Lazy eight: at the 90° point, in about 30° of bank
Both at the 90° point
Chandelle: at the 90° point. Lazy eight: at the 180° point
Chandelle: at the 180° point. Lazy eight: at the 45° point, where the pitch is highest
questions.why: A chandelle ends with the wings level, the nose high and the airspeed just above the power-on stall speed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], with the airspeed falling all the way (ACS CA.V.C.S5). In a lazy eight the airspeed is at its minimum, about 5 to 10 knots above the stall, at the 90° point, where the bank is about 30° and the pitch passes through level [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The 45° point has the highest pitch, but the airspeed is still decreasing past it while the airplane climbs [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The lazy eight's 180° point is back at entry airspeed.

questions.q: When should you first reach the highest pitch attitude in each maneuver?
options: Chandelle: at the 90° point, then hold it. Lazy eight: at the 45° point
Both at the 90° point
Chandelle: at the 45° point. Lazy eight: at the 90° point
Chandelle: at the 180° point. Lazy eight: at the 135° point
questions.why: In a chandelle the pitch rises through the first 90° so that the maximum pitch-up comes at the end of the first 90°, and that attitude is held for the rest of the maneuver [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. In a lazy eight the maximum pitch-up comes at the 45° point with about 15° of bank, and at the 90° point the pitch is passing through level [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. So 'both at 90°' is right for the chandelle only. The lazy eight's 135° point is its lowest pitch, not its highest [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

questions.q: Which Area V maneuver allows the steepest bank on the commercial checkride?
options: Chandelles, up to 45°
Steep turns, up to 55° with the tolerance
Eights on pylons, up to 60° as the AFH figure shows
Steep spiral, up to 60° at the steepest point
questions.why: The steep spiral may not exceed 60° of bank, and that limit applies at the steepest point (ACS CA.V.B.S3, S4) [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Steep turns ask for about 50° within 5°, so 55° at most (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S5). Eights on pylons is capped at 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5), even though AFH Figure 7-14 shows banks from shallow to steep [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. The chandelle bank is approximately 30° (ACS CA.V.C.S4).

questions.q: Which two Area V Tasks have no 1,500 feet AGL floor written in their commercial ACS skill elements?
options: Steep spiral and chandelles
Lazy eights and eights on pylons
Steep turns and lazy eights
Steep turns and eights on pylons
questions.why: The steep spiral, chandelle and lazy eight all name 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S6, CA.V.C.S2, CA.V.D.S2). The steep turn standards give altitude only as entry altitude within 100 feet (ACS CA.V.A.S5), so you pick a safe one yourself; a nose-low steep bank can lose a lot of altitude very quickly [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Eights on pylons is flown at the pivotal altitude, set by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]], and ground reference maneuvers are generally flown between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

questions.q: What do the rollout from a left chandelle and the rollout from the top of a left lazy eight loop have in common?
options: P-factor cancels the adverse yaw, so little rudder is needed
The airspeed is high, so the rudder can stay neutral
You roll right at low airspeed, so substantial right rudder is needed
You roll left, so left rudder is needed
questions.why: Rolling out of a left bank means rolling right. Near the slow end of a left chandelle, right rudder pressure is significant because left adverse yaw adds to left-turning tendencies such as P-factor [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The AFH sums up the lazy eight the same way: rolling right at low airspeed and high power takes substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. 'P-factor cancels the adverse yaw' is true when rolling left, as in the rollout from a right chandelle or a right lazy eight loop [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

questions.q: Using the AFH energy model, how does a chandelle differ from a lazy eight?
options: Both are pure exchanges, with the throttle left at the cruise setting
In a lazy eight you add power in each climb and take it off in each descent
In a chandelle you add power as you pitch up, adding total energy; in a lazy eight the power is set before entry and the elevator mostly trades speed and altitude back and forth
In a chandelle the elevator adds total energy and the throttle only distributes it
questions.why: The throttle is the total energy controller and the elevator is the energy distribution controller [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. In a chandelle you apply back pressure while increasing power to the recommended setting [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], so energy is added while it is moved into altitude. In a lazy eight, power is set so you do not enter above the manufacturer's speed, and too much or too little power for the bank shows up as altitude gained or lost at the end [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. In an exchange, altitude and airspeed move in opposite directions [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Saying the elevator adds total energy swaps the two controls' jobs.

questions.q: You prepared for steep turns, but the examiner picks the steep spiral. Which steep turn standard no longer applies, and what replaces it?
options: The ±10-knot airspeed tolerance; the spiral has no airspeed standard
The ±10° rollout tolerance; the spiral has no heading standard
The ±100-foot altitude tolerance; you must finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL instead
None; the spiral uses the same altitude, airspeed, bank and heading tolerances
questions.why: Steep turns are graded on entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5° and rollout ±10° (ACS CA.V.A.S5). The steep spiral keeps the specified airspeed ±10 knots and a rollout toward an object or heading ±10°, but altitude becomes a floor: finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.B.S6) [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. The bank standard changes too, to no more than 60° (ACS CA.V.B.S3), so 'the same tolerances' is wrong.

questions.q: One day the nose drops in a steep turn. Another day a steep spiral turns into a spiral dive. Which reaction is an error in both recoveries?
options: Unloading with a little forward elevator first
Pulling back on the elevator while the wings are still steeply banked
Rolling level with coordinated aileron and rudder
Reducing the bank before raising the nose
questions.why: For the nose-low steep turn, first reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose; using only the elevator steepens the bank and stresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. For a spiral dive: idle, some forward elevator to unload to about +1 G, roll level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then gently raise the nose [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Pulling out without rolling level, or pulling while rolling, are listed spiral dive recovery errors [[24:132|AFH 5-27]]. Reducing the bank first, unloading first and a coordinated roll to level are all correct steps.

questions.q: Before a steep spiral you check the POH: clean stall speed 48 knots, gliding speed 68 knots. Using the level-turn rule, what does this mean at your steepest bank of 60°?
options: Slow to 60 knots in the spiral so the margin grows
The stall speed there is about 68 knots, so there is almost no margin; pick a radius that keeps the steepest bank shallower
The margin stays about 20 knots at any bank, since stall speed is fixed
The stall speed there is about 58 knots, a comfortable 10-knot margin
questions.why: A level 60° bank gives 2.0 G, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. The square root of 2 is 1.414, and 48 x 1.414 = 67.9 knots, about the same as the 68-knot gliding speed. The AFH has you find the stall speed at the highest bank you expect before ground reference maneuvers, to be sure of a margin [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Your distance from the reference sets the radius, and the steepest bank must not exceed 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Application: a wider circle needs less bank downwind and gives back margin. Slowing down shrinks the margin, it does not grow it.

questions.q: In a high-wing trainer you will fly a left chandelle and then a steep spiral. Which clearing plan fits the sources?
options: Clear only ahead and above, since the chandelle climbs away from traffic
One set of clearing turns at the start of the flight covers both maneuvers
Before the chandelle, briefly lower the left wing and look; the spiral needs no special look below
Before the chandelle, briefly raise the left wing and look; before the spiral, look especially below you
questions.why: The PHAK says clearing should come before all turns, chandelles included, and that a high-wing pilot raises the wing in the direction of the turn and looks; lowering the wing is the low-wing technique [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]]. The AFH starts both the chandelle and the steep spiral by clearing the airspace [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. A spiral descends through the altitudes below you, and the AFH has simulated emergency descents made in a turn to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Each maneuver gets its own clearing.

questions.q: On the second lap of a steep spiral your chart slides off your lap onto the floor. What fits the sources best?
options: Look down and keep turning; disorientation cannot happen in a gliding turn
Leave it until you roll out, or get it with minimal head movement, because an abrupt head movement in a long turn can cause the Coriolis illusion
Bend down quickly and grab it; the Coriolis illusion only happens in clouds
Grab it fast; the only turning illusion is the graveyard spiral, which needs a climb
questions.why: An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create the Coriolis illusion, the most overwhelming illusion in flight; avoid sudden, extreme head movements [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. If something is dropped, retrieve it with minimal head movement and be alert for the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. The AIM says 'particularly' under IFR, not only. Becoming disoriented is also a listed steep spiral error [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Waiting until the rollout is the simplest way to avoid the head movement (application).

questions.q: Heading 360, you plan a right chandelle and then a right lazy eight. Which landmarks do you need?
options: Both: one straight ahead, since both end on the entry heading
Chandelle: one toward 090 for the 90° point and one toward 180 for the finish. Lazy eight: toward 045, 090 and 135
Chandelle: toward 270. Lazy eight: toward 315, 270 and 225
Chandelle: toward 045, 090 and 135. Lazy eight: one off the wingtip only
questions.why: The chandelle has two 90° parts: highest pitch at the 90° point, then a rollout that brings the wings level at the 180° point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], graded within 10° of that point (ACS CA.V.C.S7). Turning right from 360, those are 090 and 180. The lazy eight uses reference points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° from the starting direction for each 180° turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], so 045, 090 and 135. Neither maneuver ends its first half on the entry heading, and 270 side references belong to a left turn.

questions.q: At 100 knots groundspeed, a 45° bank gives a turn radius over the ground of about 888 feet, and the pivotal altitude rule gives about 885 feet above the pylon. Why are the two numbers nearly the same?
options: Both formulas use true airspeed, so the wind cancels out
Pivotal altitude equals the turn radius at any bank
At 45° the tangent of the bank is 1, and the height on the sight line equals the radius times the tangent of the bank
It is chance; pivotal altitude depends on bank angle and radius does not
questions.why: Radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tan bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]: 100 x 100 / (11.26 x 1) = 888 feet, matching the AFH's 890 feet at 45° and 100 knots [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. Pivotal altitude = groundspeed squared / 11.3 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]: 10,000 / 11.3 = 885 feet. Application: for the sight line along the lateral axis to meet the pylon, height = radius x tan bank, so tan bank cancels and height = speed squared / 11.26. At 45°, tan is 1, so height and radius match. At 30°, the radius is 10,000 / (11.26 x 0.577) = 1,538 feet while the pivotal height is still 885, so they are not equal at every bank. The bank does not alter the pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

questions.q: Your chandelle ends with the wings level on the 180° point, but the airspeed is still 20 knots above the stall. What should you change next time?
options: Keep raising the pitch through the second 90°
Raise the pitch higher by the 90° point, then hold it
Use a steeper bank, about 45°
Roll out faster in the second 90°
questions.why: 'Pitch attitude is low on recovery resulting in airspeed well above stall speed' is a listed chandelle error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. If the pitch is set too low, the airspeed never decreases to just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], so the fix is more pitch by the 90° point. Raising the pitch during the second 90° is its own listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and the ACS asks for a constant pitch there (ACS CA.V.C.S6). A bank that is too steep fails to get maximum performance [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and a faster rollout only throws off the heading [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: You roll into a chandelle at only 20° of bank. With about 140° of the turn done, the airspeed is nearly gone. What is this, and what is the safe action?
options: Initial bank too steep; hold the nose up to finish the 180°
Initial bank too shallow; lower the nose and accept the heading error rather than stall
Nothing is wrong; keep the pitch even if it stalls at 180°
Pitch too low; pull harder to reach the 180° point
questions.why: 'Initial bank is too shallow resulting in a stall' is a listed chandelle error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Rate of turn rises with the tangent of the bank [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]], so a shallow bank turns slowly and the speed runs out before the heading comes around (application). The ACS wants the finish just above a stall airspeed, avoiding a stall (ACS CA.V.C.S7), and stalling at any point is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. A heading miss is the smaller fault, so lower the nose.

questions.q: You normally fly from the left seat of a high-wing trainer. Today you fly eights on pylons from the right seat. What reference do you use?
options: The same strut mark you use from the left seat
A line from your eyes parallel to the lateral axis, found again for this seat; it may not lie on the wingtip
The wingtip, since it marks the reference in every airplane
Whatever point keeps the pylon straight below the wing
questions.why: The reference is an imaginary line from your eyes to the pylon, parallel to the lateral axis [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. The AFH says the 'wingtip' version is not correct, because wing and seat designs give different angles from the eye to the wingtip, and the line differs for each pilot and from each seat [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. A mark found from the left seat for left turns does not carry over to the other seat and side, so find it again.

questions.q: At the 135° point of a lazy eight half, what should the airplane show?
options: Highest pitch attitude, about 15° of bank, airspeed decreasing
Lowest pitch attitude, about 15° of bank, airspeed increasing
Pitch passing through level, about 30° of bank, slowest airspeed
Wings level at entry airspeed and altitude
questions.why: When the airplane has turned 135°, it should be at its lowest pitch attitude, and the airspeed is increasing as the pitch decreases, so less right rudder is needed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Figure 10-4 shows about 15° of bank at that point [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Highest pitch with the speed falling is the 45° point, level pitch at 30° and the slowest speed is the 90° point, and wings level at entry airspeed and altitude is the 180° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

questions.q: You learned steep turns at 45° for your private certificate. On the commercial checkride you hold exactly 45° all the way around. How does that compare with the ACS?
options: It fails, since the commercial ACS asks for 60°
It fails, since the commercial standard is 50° ±2°
Inside the tolerance, but right at its lower edge; the target is about 50°
It is ideal, since both ACS documents ask for 45°
questions.why: The commercial ACS asks for approximately a 50° bank (ACS CA.V.A.S3) held within 5° (ACS CA.V.A.S5), so 45° to 55° passes. The private ACS asks for approximately 45° (ACS PA.V.A.S3). The AFH gives steep turns a bank between 45° and 60° [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At exactly 45°, any drift shallower fails, so aim for 50°.
